## The trap

You look at a hot statement in `pg_stat_statements` and see a run of bare boolean parameters:

```
WHERE workspace_id = $1 AND kind = ANY($2::text[]) AND state = $3
  AND $6 AND $7 AND $8 AND $9 ... AND $23
```

Eighteen consecutive opaque booleans. The natural reading is that the application passes optional filters as **protocol bind parameters** — either a real condition or a no-op `true` — so the planner sees values it cannot inspect, cannot use to select an index, and cannot use to prune early. That yields a confident diagnosis: *non-sargable; scans broadly and truncates; build the WHERE clause dynamically.*

It is wrong, and it is wrong in a way that survives review, because the evidence looks like a direct reading of production behaviour.

## What is actually true

`pg_stat_statements` stores a **normalized** statement. It replaces *every constant* with `$n` — not only protocol binds. Literal `TRUE`, literal `FALSE` and literal integers all normalize identically.

Measured directly on this box (2026-09-01) by submitting a marked statement and reading back how pgss chose to store it:

| submitted | stored by pg_stat_statements |
|---|---|
| `SELECT 1 AS marker WHERE TRUE AND TRUE AND 1 = 1` | `SELECT $1 AS marker WHERE $2 AND $3 AND $4 = $5` |

Literal `TRUE` became `$2` and `$3`; literal `1 = 1` became `$4 = $5`. So `AND $6 AND $7` in a pgss entry is **fully consistent with source that emits `AND TRUE AND TRUE`** — the text cannot distinguish the two cases.

That is exactly what the issues reader does. Every inactive predicate is emitted as a literal `TRUE` fragment (`issues-engineer.ts`, the `listIssues` WHERE builder):

```ts
AND ${filter.state    ? sql`ei.state = ${filter.state}`                    : sql`TRUE`}
AND ${filter.scopes   ? sql`ei.scope = ANY(${filter.scopes}::text[])`      : sql`TRUE`}
AND ${filter.severities ? sql`ei.severity = ANY(${...}::text[])`          : sql`TRUE`}
```

Postgres **constant-folds literal `TRUE` at plan time**: `WHERE a AND TRUE AND TRUE` is planned identically to `WHERE a`. There is no opaque value, no lost index selection, and nothing to repair.

## Why it matters

The obvious remedy — *"build the WHERE clause dynamically so only ACTIVE predicates appear"* — changes only how the statement **renders in pgss**. It cannot improve the plan, because the planner has already discarded those conjuncts. Implementing it is pure churn at every site it touches, and it is the kind of churn that looks like a performance win in the commit message.

WI-878964 filed precisely this against `harness_shared.engineer_issues` (112,742 calls, 2.09 s mean, "2.6% of ALL database execution time") and proposed the dynamic-WHERE fix as a class, asserting *"same root pattern as the 4 sites in `agent-tools/plans/source.ts` — worth fixing as one class."* The premise was false at all of them.

## How to tell the difference

Never diagnose sargability from pgss text. Instead:

1. **Read the source that builds the statement.** Does the inactive branch emit a literal (`` sql`TRUE` ``) or interpolate a value? Only the second is a real bind.
2. **`EXPLAIN` the real query** with real arguments and read the chosen plan. That is the only authority on index selection.
3. **Re-probe empirically** when unsure — submit a distinctively-marked statement containing a literal and read back its stored text (the recipe above takes one call and is definitive).

## A related non-bug: `rows/calls` pinned at exactly the LIMIT

The same filing flagged `rows/calls = EXACTLY 500.0` across every call as "the signature of a LIMIT cap hit every single time… callers may be reading a truncated answer as a complete one."

The *measurement* is real and worth keeping — a ratio pinned to the cap does mean the filtered set always exceeds it. But it is **not automatically a defect**. Before concluding truncation harm, check whether the caller pairs the capped list with an **uncapped count**:

- `agent-tools/harness/overview.ts` fetches `listIssues({ limit })` alongside `countIssues(filter)` — the capped list is presentational, the total is true.
- `harness/improvements/read-items.ts` pushes its scope/origin predicates into SQL (its JS post-filters are documented *defensive duplicates*, not the filter itself) and has a paired `countImprovementItems` built expressly so callers do not aggregate over whatever the read happened to fetch.

Both are the correct pattern. The genuine defect of this shape is the one WI-4532 fixed: a caller that wants a *set*, fetches `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT n`, and then **post-filters in JS** — which silently yields "matching rows among the n newest", a recency window rather than a set. The discriminator is *where the filter runs*, not the ratio.

## The neighbouring pgss trap

A different misreading of the same table is covered separately in
[a "coord_event_log furnace" EI is usually stale pg_stat_statements debris](/internal/docs/agent-insights/coord-log-furnace-ei-is-usually-stale-pgss-debris):
pgss aggregates over the whole window since the last reset, so a statement fixed weeks ago keeps its catastrophic lifetime `mean_exec_time` forever. Together these are the two standing ways a pgss reading manufactures a bug that is not there — one from **normalized text**, one from **stale aggregates**.
